background.definition: Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency is an autosomal co-dominant condition affecting lung, liver, and rarely skin. The most important complication is chronic lung disease, especially in smokers.

list.listitem: Reported incidence in whites is 1 in 2000 to 1 in 3000 live births.
The estimated prevalence is 1 case per 3000 to 5000 persons in the United States.
AAT deficiency is more prevalent in people of northern and western European descent.
In a study of 1044 COPD patients from Spain and Germany, 4.1% were heterozygotes and 0.3% were homozygous.
The prevalence is only 0.5% among patients with bronchiectasis in the UK.
A total of 2% to 3% of patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) have AAT deficiency.
In newborns with AAT deficiency, 17% have symptoms of liver disease in infancy and 2.5% die of cirrhosis by age 18 years.
Cirrhosis of the liver occurs in approximately 5% to 15% of AAT-deficient individuals.
AAT deficiency is due to a genetic defect in the SERPINA1 gene located on chromosome 14q31-32.3.
AAT is a glycoprotein synthesized mainly by hepatocytes. AAT protects tissue from damage by proteolytic enzymes, especially neutrophil elastase.

AAT is a encoded by the SERPINA1 gene located on chromosome segment 14q31-32.3. There are more than 100 alleles. The alleles are further grouped based on their ability to produce AAT: normal, deficient, null, and dysfunctional.

Most persons are homozygous for MM phenotype and produce normal amounts of AAT. The most common abnormal genes are S and Z alleles. In patients homozygous for ZZ alleles, 85% of synthesized AAT is blocked in the terminal secretory pathway of the hepatocyte.
Deficiency or absence of AAT results in unchecked activity of elastase in the lung, causing emphysema. The unsecreted and polymerized AAT results in damage to the liver.
In the null variants of AAT deficiency, no AAT protein is produced resulting in severe disease.
Dysfunctional alleles produce normal quantities of AAT protein, but the AAT protein does not function normally.

Population screening is not generally recommended. It may be considered in countries where there is a high prevalence (1/1500) and high smoking rates, and where adequate counseling regarding implications of diagnosis is available. C
Patients should be counseled to quit smoking and avoid environmental pollutants like second-hand smoke, dusts, and fumes. C
Influenza and pneumococcal vaccination are recommended, as well as vaccination against hepatitis B for patients with AAT deficiency and liver disease. C
Check serum AAT levels in patients where there is a high degree of suspicion (). B
Confirm the diagnosis of AAT deficiency by genetic testing. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Spirometry showing obstructive pattern and evidence of reversibility on bronchodialation
Spirometry showing obstructive pattern but not fully reversible on bronchodialation
Transthoracic echocardiograph showing systolic or diastolic dysfunction
High-resolution CT scan of the chest with ground glass appearance
History of excessive alcohol use and ultrasonography of the liver showing changes consistent with cirrhosis
Viral serology showing hepatitis B surface antigen or presence of antihepatitis C antibody
Decreased serum ceruloplasmin and increased free copper

list.listitem: See for patients in whom AAT deficiency should be considered.

Dyspnea on exertion is the most frequent presenting symptom (84%), and wheezing (76%) is also common in patients with AAT deficiency and lung involvement. Cough with and without expectoration is seen in approximately 50% of patients.
AAT-deficient individuals can also present with allergic rhinitis (35%) or with episodic wheezing with dyspnea consistent with asthma (22%).

Individuals with homozygous AAT deficiency can present with neonatal obstructive jaundice (12%) or abnormal liver function test results (18%) Cirrhosis of liver may be seen, most often after the age of 50 years.

Weight loss, fatigue, abdominal distension, and pain may also be present. No physical examination findings are characteristic for AAT and patients may have a normal physical examination. Or, patients may present with typical findings of COPD, such as an asthenic appearance with barrel-shaped chest, reduced breath sounds, rhonchi, and prolonged expiratory wheeze.

Patients with liver involvement may present with jaundice, spider nevi, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and peripheral edema. Skin manifestations are rare (1 in 1000) and may present as painful red nodules on thighs or buttocks in young adults. Nodules (necrotizing panniculitis) may ulcerate with drainage of clear yellow odorless fluid.
Order a serum quantitative AAT level in patients with a high degree of clinical suspicion ().
The yield is low among patients with bronchiectasis in the UK (8 with AAT in a series of 1600 or 0.5%).
A lateral flow assay was 74% sensitive and 98% specific for AAT compared with genetic testing, with a positive predictive value of 58% in an unselected group of patients with COPD.
Serum phenotyping (genetic testing) by isoelectric focusing is the definitive test for diagnosing AAT deficiency, and should be ordered when serum AAT levels are less than 120 mg/dL (11µM/L).
Order hepatic transaminases, tests of hepatic function, and a chest x-ray in patients with confirmed AAT deficiency.

Patients with AAT deficiency and lung involvement should also have the following tests to assess the severity of disease and possible complications: chest x-ray, pulmonary function tests, arterial blood gases and gas transfer, and chest CT.

Patients with AAT deficiency and liver involvement should have the following tests: viral hepatitis serology, serum transferrin and ceruloplasmin levels, ultrasound of the liver, and (if appropriate) liver biopsy to stage severity of liver disease.
See for a list of patients at higher than average risk for AAT deficiency.
In the presence of any of the above features, order serum AAT levels and confirm the diagnosis by genetic testing.
AAT augmentation therapy is indicated in patients with serum AAT levels of less than 120 mg/dL (11 µM/L) or if FEV1 is 30% to 65% of predicted. B
Consider organ transplant in patients with end-stage liver disease or lung disease. C

Augmentation therapy with intravenous infusion of AAT once a week may reduce decline in lung function. A systematic review of 26 studies found that it slowed the decline in CT density. However, the effect on clinical outcomes is not known.Indications for consideration of augmentation therapy include an AAT level of less than 120 mg/dL (11 µM/L) or a decline in FEV1 (postbronchodialation) between 30% and 65% of predicted. AAT treatment is currently not recommended for patients without emphysema.
AAT augmentation therapy either alone or combined with dapsone is effective in treatment of necrotizing panniculitis.
Other treatments like aerosol AAT augmentation, recombinant AAT augmentation, and synthetic low-molecular leukoprotease inhibitors are being evaluated.

Fazirsiran is an RNA interference drug that degrades AAT and Z-AAT messenger RNA, and reduces their synthesis in liver cells. A Phase 2 study gave the drug to 16 patients with PI ZZ genotype and liver fibrosis on day 1, week 4, and then every 12 weeks by subcutaneous injection. They saw regression of fibrosis in 7 of 15 patients and large reductions in Z-AAT levels in the liver.

Antibiotics should be used in patients with bronchitis or upper respiratory tract infection. Early antibiotic treatment is recommended for all purulent exacerbations as infection causes increased elastolytic burden in patients with AAT deficiency.
Patients with AAT deficiency and lung involvement may benefit from inhaled bronchodialators and inhaled steroids.
Consider lung transplantation in patients with end-stage lung disease.
Consider liver transplantation in those with advanced liver disease.
Pulmonary rehabilitation combined with cardiovascular fitness reduces dyspnea and the number of hospitalizations in individuals with functional impairment.
Oxygen should be used in patients who desaturate on exertion. In patients with severe hypoxemia, long-term oxygen therapy should be started according to American Thoracic Society guidelines.
In patients with AAT deficiency and lung involvement who continue to smoke, life expectancy is less than 20 years from diagnosis. B
Patients with chronic liver disease and AAT deficiency have poor prognosis and lower life expectancy. B
The overall mortality in patients with severe deficiency is approximately 3% per year. B
Liver disease affects 10% to 15% of newborns with severe AAT deficiency. They may develop cholestasis between 4 days and 4 months after birth, which may persist for up to 12 months.
Some may develop cirrhosis between the ages 6 months to 11 years, or they may have persistent elevation of aminotransferases without the development of cirrhosis.
Adults older than 50 years without childhood liver disease may develop cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma.
The natural history of the disease after the first 2 decades of life is less clear. Some patients may develop decline in lung function and smokers have a high risk of developing COPD.
However, asymptomatic individuals who do not smoke can have a normal life span.
Among lung transplant recipients, lung function declined at a rate similar to that of COPD patients with normal AAT levels.
The annual mortality rate in patients with severe deficiency is approximately 3% per year.
Increasing age, lower educational level, lung transplants, and lower initial FEV1 are associated with higher mortality.
Mortality in homozygotes with AAT deficiency who do not smoke is similar to that of the general population.
In patients with AAT deficiency and lung involvement who continue to smoke, life expectancy is less than 20 years from diagnosis.
Survival after lung transplant is better for patients with end-stage COPD and severe AAT than it is for those with tobacco-related COPD.
Pregnant patients with AAT (PI ZZ) deficiency have an increased frequency of miscarriage and stillbirth.
